title: Spain and Portugal
description: An ageing system written into law, high plateaus, a green Atlantic coast and Portugal's native grapes.
L: Explain why ageing is part of Spanish style

Spain sets national minimum ageing for its terms. For reds: Crianza, at least 24 months, 6 in oak; Reserva, 36 months, 12 in oak; Gran Reserva, 60 months, 18 in oak. Some regions are stricter: in Rioja, Crianza needs 12 months in oak and Gran Reserva 24. Joven means young, with little or no oak.

Spain's PDO wines include DO and the higher DOCa, only Rioja and Priorat, called DOQ in Catalan. Vino de Pago is for single estates with their own appellation. Vino de la Tierra is the PGI level. Since 2015, smaller areas like village wines can be named, and Rioja recognises single vineyards, called Viñedo Singular.
DOCa, DO, Vino de Pago, Vino de la Tierra
Order these Spanish ageing terms from shortest to longest minimum ageing.
Each step adds time in oak and bottle.

Spanish bodegas long aged wine before release, so consumers got it ready to drink. Traditional Rioja spent years in American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill, with soft, mature fruit. Many modern producers use less time and more French oak, and the ageing terms are now only one style choice among many.
Which Spanish regions hold the top DOCa status?
Only Rioja and Priorat have DOCa, written DOQ in Catalan for Priorat.
Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva set minimum ageing
DOCa is Spain's top level, held by Rioja and Priorat
Spanish wines were traditionally released ready to drink

Rioja runs along the Ebro river in northern Spain. It has three sub-zones: Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, cooler and higher, with Atlantic influence, and Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja, warmer and Mediterranean. Tempranillo leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo, which is Carignan. Whites use Viura.

Traditional Rioja blends grapes from across sub-zones and ages them long in used American oak, giving pale, mellow wines with vanilla and dried fruit. Since the 1990s, modern producers have used French oak, riper fruit, shorter ageing and single vineyards, giving darker, fruitier wines. Both styles thrive today.
American oak and time, or French oak and fruit
Which sub-zone of Rioja is warmest and most Mediterranean?
Rioja Oriental, to the east, is warmer and drier, suiting Garnacha.

Navarra, just north-east of Rioja, was long known for Garnacha rosado. Today it makes reds from Tempranillo, Garnacha and Bordeaux grapes, and fresh whites. Its climate runs from Atlantic in the north to dry Mediterranean in the south.
Which grapes are permitted in red Rioja?
Nebbiolo is a Piedmont grape. Rioja's reds use Tempranillo, Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo.
Rioja has three sub-zones and is led by Tempranillo
Traditional Rioja uses American oak and long ageing; modern uses French oak
Navarra moved from rosado to varied reds and whites
Explain the role of altitude on the Meseta

Ribera del Duero sits on Spain's central plateau, the Meseta, at 750 to 1,000 m. Tempranillo, called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País, gives deep, powerful reds. Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864, made the name; the 1980s brought international fame. Hot days and very cold nights give ripe fruit with fresh acidity.

The Meseta is high and continental. Summer days can reach 35 degrees, while nights drop below 15, a wide diurnal range that keeps acidity. Winters are harsh and spring frosts are a constant risk; Ribera lost much of its 2017 crop to frost. Old bush vines on poor soils give low yields.
Hot days, cold nights, frost risk
Match each Duero wine to its grape.
The same river crosses Spain and Portugal, with different grapes on each side.

Toro, further west and lower, makes very ripe, powerful reds from Tinta de Toro, a local form of Tempranillo. Rueda is the Duero's white wine region, making crisp, aromatic Verdejo with fennel, citrus and herbs, often blended with Sauvignon Blanc. Many Rueda grapes are picked at night to stay cool.
Rueda is best known for red wines.
Not true. Rueda is the Duero's white wine region, built on Verdejo.
Ribera del Duero makes powerful Tinto Fino at high altitude
Hot days, cold nights and frost shape the Meseta
Toro makes ripe reds; Rueda makes Verdejo whites

North-west Spain, Galicia and the Basque Country, is Atlantic, with rainfall over 1,500 mm a year in places. It's called green Spain. Vines are often trained high on granite pergolas, called parras, to keep grapes away from damp ground. Wines are fresh, light and aromatic.

Rías Baixas, on Galicia's coast, is built on Albariño, about 96% of plantings. Thick skins resist mildew. The wines have peach, citrus and a saline edge, usually unoaked. There are five sub-zones, including Val do Salnés, the coolest and wettest, and O Rosal, along the Miño river border with Portugal.
Why is Albariño well suited to Rías Baixas?
Its thick skins resist mildew in the damp climate
Thick skins protect against rot and mildew in one of Spain's wettest regions.

Ribeira Sacra grows Mencía on steep, terraced slopes above the Sil river, giving fresh, floral reds. Valdeorras makes Godello, a textured, mineral white. In the Basque Country, Txakoli is a light, slightly sparkling white from Hondarrabi Zuri, traditionally poured from a height.
Which wines come from green Spain?
Priorat is in Catalonia, in the dry north-east.
Green Spain is wet and Atlantic, with high-trained vines
Rías Baixas is built on thick-skinned Albariño
Mencía, Godello and Txakoli complete the north-west
Name the main wines of the Levante

Most Cava comes from Penedès, near Barcelona, made by the traditional method. The main grapes are Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada. Minimum ageing on lees is 9 months; Reserva needs 18 months and Gran Reserva 30. Some producers left the Cava DO to form Corpinnat and Clàssic Penedès, with stricter rules.

Priorat, south-west of Barcelona, revived in the late 1980s when a group of producers, including René Barbier and Álvaro Palacios, made powerful reds from old Garnacha and Cariñena. Vines grow on steep slopes of llicorella, a dark slate that forces roots deep and keeps yields tiny. It became a DOCa in 2000.
Llicorella slate, old Garnacha and Cariñena
Match each wine to its grapes.
Each region of eastern Spain has its own grape identity.

South of Valencia, the Levante is hot and dry. Jumilla and Yecla make ripe, powerful reds from Monastrell, the same grape as Mourvèdre. Alicante makes reds and a rare sweet wine, Fondillón. Valencia makes everything from bulk wine to sweet Moscatel.
Priorat's llicorella is a dark slate soil.
Yes. It forces roots deep and keeps yields very low, giving concentrated wines.
Cava is mostly from Penedès, made by the traditional method
Priorat grows old Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate
The Levante makes ripe Monastrell reds
Describe the Douro and its two wines

Vinho Verde, in the green north-west, has heavy rainfall and granite soils. It makes light, fresh, sometimes slightly spritzy whites from Loureiro, Arinto, Avesso and Alvarinho. Monção e Melgaço, along the Minho river, is the home of Alvarinho, making fuller, more serious whites. Verde means green, for youth and the landscape.

The Douro valley, upstream, is hot and dry, with schist soils and terraces carved into steep slopes. It was demarcated in 1756, among the world's first wine regions to be legally defined. It makes Port and, increasingly, dry reds from Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz. UNESCO listed it as World Heritage in 2001.
When was the Douro demarcated as a wine region?
The Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro in 1756, among the earliest legal wine regions.

The Dão, south of the Douro, is ringed by mountains that block both Atlantic rain and continental heat. Granite soils and altitude, 200 to 900 m, give fresh, elegant wines. Touriga Nacional, Jaen and Alfrocheiro make the reds, and Encruzado makes fine, age-worthy whites.
Match each region to its signature wine.
Portugal's north moves from green and rainy to hot and dry.
Vinho Verde makes fresh whites; Monção e Melgaço is Alvarinho's home
The Douro makes Port and dry reds on schist terraces
The Dão is mountain-ringed, granite and elegant
Explain the importance of native grapes

Bairrada, near the coast, has clay and limestone soils and makes tannic reds from Baga, and traditional method sparkling wines. Lisboa, north of the capital, is Atlantic and productive, with Bucelas for Arinto whites and Colares, where vines grow ungrafted in sand dunes by the sea, protected from phylloxera.
Baga in Bairrada; Colares in the sand

The Alentejo covers much of southern Portugal: hot, dry, with wide plains. Its reds are ripe and fruity, from Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, a red-fleshed grape. Whites use Antão Vaz. Some producers still ferment in talhas, large clay pots, a Roman tradition that the DOC now recognises as Vinho de Talha.
Colares vines grow ungrafted because phylloxera cannot survive in sandy soils.
Yes. Phylloxera struggles to move through sand, so Colares vines grow on their own roots.

Portugal has around 250 native grapes, and few international ones. Many are known by different names: Tempranillo is Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo. Field blends, with many varieties mixed in old vineyards, are common. This diversity gives Portugal a distinct identity.
What is unusual about Alicante Bouschet?
Alicante Bouschet is a teinturier, with red flesh, giving very deep colour.
Bairrada makes Baga reds and sparkling wines; Colares grows ungrafted in sand
The Alentejo makes ripe reds and keeps the talha tradition
Explain Spain's ageing and quality system
Link Iberian regions to their grapes
Compare north and south in both countries
Order Spain's red ageing categories from youngest to oldest.
Each category requires more time in oak and bottle.
Match each region to its main grape.
Iberia's regions each have their own identity.
Llicorella forces roots deep and keeps yields tiny.
In the Alentejo, Tempranillo is called Aragonez.
Yes. In the Douro it's Tinta Roriz; in Spain, Tempranillo or Tinto Fino.
Spain's ageing terms run from Joven to Gran Reserva
Rioja and Priorat are Spain's DOCa regions
Green Iberia makes fresh whites; the plateau and the south make ripe reds
Portugal's native grapes give it a unique identity
